title: Governance-ready AI in mental health.
authors: Balcombe L, De Leo D, Andrisano Ruggieri R, Ragosta A, Kannis-Dymand L.
abstract:
Objective

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots increasingly function as an informal, de facto source of mental health support. This paper develops a governance framework for associated harms and specifies requirements for governance-ready design and evaluation.

Method

We conducted a purposive narrative review across seven databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar; searches through July 2026) using structured search query strings. Empirical evidence was systematically categorised and distinguished from theoretical psychoanalytic constructs. Findings informed a foundational design analysis of Eva, an unvalidated research case architecture informed by lived experience input.

Results

We distinguish acute Type I harms (single-turn technical failures) from cumulative Type II harms (multi-session relational risks), characterised through digital psychological harm, the uncanny setting, relational hallucination, algorithmic collusion, AI-mediated psychosis, and epistemic exploitation. Governance-by-design responses include the SAFE-AI (i.e., Screening, Alignment, Facilitation, and Evaluation of AI-Enhanced Interventions) protocol, empathy by design, suitability screening, psychodynamic transcript analytics, bounded co-regulation, data sovereignty, and crisis-safe escalation rather than simulated therapy.

Conclusions

The central proposition of this paper is that generative AI may support mental health care only when bounded by governance-by-design, clinically informed safety mechanisms, and accountable human oversight, and only once these safeguards have been independently validated. Specifically, we identify three sets of conditions for governance-ready GenAI: clinical conditions, including suitability screening and crisis-safe escalation; relational conditions, including bounded roles, anti-collusive friction, and longitudinal monitoring of Type II drift; and operational conditions, including human oversight, data sovereignty, auditability, and independent validation.
